analysis.one_liner: Removes the antitrust law exemption that shields health insurers from price-fixing suits.
analysis.headline: The bill never left the Senate Judiciary Committee and died without a vote at the end of 2020.
analysis.plain_summary: Since 1945, federal antitrust laws have not applied to the insurance industry under the McCarran-Ferguson Act, so health insurers could agree with each other on prices without facing antitrust lawsuits. This bill would make antitrust laws apply to health and dental insurance again, while keeping a carve-out so insurers could still share claims data and use standard policy forms. It died in committee without ever getting a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers who buy health or dental insurance, if removing the exemption leads insurers to compete more on price. Enforcers like the Justice Department and Federal Trade Commission would also gain authority over insurer conduct.

how_it_helps.text: The bill amends the McCarran-Ferguson Act so that nothing in it impairs or supersedes the antitrust laws with respect to the business of health insurance, including dental insurance [S3].
It applies prohibitions against unfair methods of competition under section 5 of the Federal Trade Commission Act to health insurance whether or not the business is carried on for profit [S2].

The carve-outs are narrow: insurers may still collaborate to collect historical loss data, determine loss development factors, perform actuarial services, and use standard policy forms, so long as that work does not restrain trade [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Health insurers, which would face antitrust liability for colluding on prices or dividing markets, and could pass new litigation and compliance costs into premiums.

drawbacks.text: The bill preserves broad carve-outs for data collection, actuarial work, and standard policy forms, so the core practice critics say matters most — insurers sharing claims data — would continue under a legal safe harbor [S2].

Insurers have long argued that pooling of claims data helps small and regional carriers price their policies accurately, and that new antitrust exposure could raise administrative costs that show up in premiums; the bill does not address how any cost increases would be contained.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill would close a genuine gap: federal antitrust law does not reach health insurance today, so insurers can coordinate on prices and market division without legal consequence. Its main limitation is that it leaves in place a safe harbor for the industry's data-sharing and standard-setting activities, so the practical change may be narrower than the headline. Still, restoring antitrust enforcement against outright price-fixing in a market nearly every household deals with outweighs the modest administrative costs insurers would face.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate Judiciary Committee, which never acted on it, so it died when that Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Steve Daines introduced the bill with Sen. Patrick Leahy on February 6, 2019, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on the Judiciary [S5].
The bill's only action was that referral; the record shows no hearing, no committee vote, and no floor action for the rest of the 116th Congress [S5].
The bill drew six cosponsors, split evenly between three Democrats and three Republicans [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Health insurers, which kept their exemption from federal antitrust law and faced no new liability for price coordination. Consumers got nothing from the bill's death.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Health insurers, who kept their antitrust exemption

industries.note: The bill would strip health and dental insurers of their exemption from federal antitrust law, exposing them to suits for price-fixing and market allocation. Today they can coordinate on prices without that liability, which consumers ultimately pay for in premiums.

Even while targeting insurers generally, the bill writes a legal safe harbor into law for collecting loss data, setting loss development factors, actuarial work, and standard policy forms. That locks in the industry's existing data-pooling arrangements as a permanent exception to antitrust rules.
